This guide walks you through a complete RiboPilot project, from raw sequencing
reads to a finished, GenBank-ready nuclear ribosomal repeat (nrDNA). It is
written for biologists. You do **not** need programming experience: you will type
a handful of short commands into R (mostly to start things), but the review and
clean-up work happens in a point-and-click app in your web browser.

If you already use [MitoPilot](https://github.com/Smithsonian/MitoPilot), this
will feel familiar. The two tools work the same way, use the same input files,
and can run on the same samples.

# How RiboPilot works, in brief

Every cell copies its ribosomal RNA genes in a repeated unit, hundreds to
thousands of times in a row. Even shallow, inexpensive "genome skim" sequencing
therefore captures this region very deeply. RiboPilot reconstructs the repeat:

```
   ETS   18S    ITS1   5.8S   ITS2    28S     IGS
 --|===|=======|~~~~~|=====|~~~~~|===========|------ (repeated hundreds of times)
       SSU              LSU
```

It reports five parts of that repeat for each sample: the three conserved
ribosomal genes (**18S, 5.8S, 28S**) and the two fast-evolving spacers between
them (**ITS1, ITS2**). The genes are easy to find and act as landmarks; the
spacers are simply the stretches between those landmarks, and they are the
regions most useful for telling closely related species apart.

A project moves through four stages, and RiboPilot keeps track of where every
sample is:

1. **Assemble** the repeat for each sample.
2. **Annotate** it (mark the five features).
3. **Review and curate** the results in the app.
4. **Export** a submission package.

# Step 0: One-time setup

Before your first project, three things need to be installed. This is usually
done once, and lab or institutional computing staff can help if any of it is
unfamiliar.

- **R** (version 4.4.0 or newer): the environment you will type commands into.
- **Nextflow**: the engine that runs the analysis steps.
- **The analysis tools** RiboPilot relies on. The simplest way to get all of them
  is with **conda**, which installs a self-contained bundle of programs (called an
  "environment") that will not interfere with anything else on your computer.
  After installing conda, run these two lines in a terminal to create the
  RiboPilot environment named `ribopilot`:

```bash
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate ribopilot
```

Then install RiboPilot itself, from within R:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("dmacguigan/RiboPilot")
```

<div class="alert alert-note">
<strong>Tip.</strong> Start R from a terminal where you have already run
<code>conda activate ribopilot</code>. That way RiboPilot can find all the tools
it needs. Alternatively, tell each command which environment to use by adding
<code>conda_env = "ribopilot"</code>, as shown throughout this guide.
</div>

<div class="alert alert-note">
An <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/docs/v2/api/api-keys/">NCBI API
key</a> is optional but recommended. It is a free code from NCBI that lets
RiboPilot look up reference sequences faster and more reliably. You paste it in
when you create a project (below).
</div>

# Step 1: Try the practice project first

RiboPilot ships a small set of fish samples so you can confirm everything works
before using your own data. One command downloads the samples and sets up a ready
-to-run project:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::new_test_project(path = "~/ribopilot_test", executor = "conda")
```

This downloads a few gigabytes of data, so it can take a while. When it finishes,
you have a working project you can practice on using the steps below. We strongly
recommend doing this once before starting with your own samples.

# Step 2: Reference data for your group of organisms

To assemble a sample, RiboPilot compares the reads to known ribosomal sequences
from related organisms. It comes ready to use for **ray-finned fishes**. If your
samples are fish, you can skip to Step 3.

For any other group, RiboPilot can build the reference data it needs by
downloading published sequences from GenBank. You do this once per group, and the
result is reused for every future project on that group. For example, for
gastropods (snails and slugs):

```{r, purl = FALSE}
# First, just see how many sequences are available (nothing is downloaded yet):
RiboPilot::build_reference_db(
  '"Gastropoda"[Organism]', "gastropoda",
  count_only = TRUE, conda_env = "ribopilot"
)

# Then build the reference data and save it somewhere you can reuse it:
db <- RiboPilot::build_reference_db(
  '"Gastropoda"[Organism]', "gastropoda",
  out_dir = "~/ribopilot_refs", conda_env = "ribopilot"
)
```

The first value in quotes is a standard NCBI search. Replace `Gastropoda` with
your group's name. The [reference database guide](Reference-Databases.html) has
more detail and tips for groups with few available sequences.

# Step 3: Set up your project

A project starts with a **mapping file** and one command. The mapping file is a
spreadsheet saved as CSV that lists your samples. It needs at least these columns:

- `ID`: a short, unique name for each sample
- `Taxon`: the species or genus name
- `R1` and `R2`: the two file names holding that sample's paired sequencing reads

You can add any other columns you like (for example a museum voucher or BioSample
number). RiboPilot keeps them and can add them to your GenBank submission later.

Create the project with `new_project()`:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path       = "~/my_project",       # where to create the project folder
  mapping_fn = "~/my_samples.csv",   # your mapping file
  data_path  = "~/my_reads",         # folder containing the read files
  executor   = "conda",
  ncbi_api_key = "PASTE_YOUR_KEY_HERE"
)
```

If you built reference data in Step 2 for a non-fish group, point the project at
it by adding these two lines inside the parentheses:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
  custom_seeds_db  = db$seeds,
  custom_labels_db = db$labels
```

This creates a project folder containing your sample list and RiboPilot's
tracking file. From here on, everything refers to that folder.

<div class="alert alert-note">
<code>executor = "conda"</code> tells RiboPilot to run on your own computer using
the tools you installed with conda. If your lab uses a shared computing cluster,
there are other options; see the function help for
<code>new_project()</code> and <code>generate_config()</code>, or ask your
computing support staff.
</div>

# Step 4: Assemble your samples

One command runs the assembly stage: it cleans the reads, assembles the
ribosomal repeat for each sample, picks the best reconstruction, and prepares the
review aids (a closest-match GenBank search and a sequencing-depth profile).

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::run_assembly("~/my_project", conda_env = "ribopilot")
```

This is the longest step, because it does real work for every sample. You can let
it run and come back later. When it finishes, every sample has an assembly ready
for your review. Annotation happens later, in a separate step, only after you
have reviewed and approved the assemblies (this is deliberate: there is no point
annotating a reconstruction you have not yet accepted).

<div class="alert alert-note">
Part of this step tries to look up the closest published match on NCBI to help
with quality checking. If NCBI is unreachable or slow, RiboPilot simply skips that
lookup and carries on; your assemblies and annotations are not affected.
</div>

# Step 5: Rescue difficult samples (optional)

A few samples, especially shallow or unusual ones, may not assemble on the first
pass. RiboPilot can make a second attempt at just those samples using a
different assembler, which fishes out the reads that look like ribosomal DNA
first and then assembles only those. It is the same assembly step as before, so
everything after it works exactly the same way:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::run_fallback("~/my_project", conda_env = "ribopilot")
```

You can skip this and come back to it later if you prefer.

# Step 6: Review and lock the assemblies

This is where most of your time is spent, and it is entirely point-and-click.
Open the app from R:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot("~/my_project")
```

The app opens in your web browser as a table with one row per sample, organized
into three tabs that follow the workflow: **Assemble**, **Annotate**, and
**Export**. Each row shows an icon for the sample's status and whether it is
**locked**. Locking a sample "signs off" on it and moves it to the next stage: a
sample must be locked in the Assemble tab before it can be annotated, and locked
in the Annotate tab before it can be exported. You can select several rows and
lock them together.

Work in the **Assemble tab**: look at each sample's reconstruction (RiboPilot has
already chosen what it thinks is the best one), check it against the sequencing
depth and the closest GenBank match, switch to an alternative reconstruction or
adjust the exact endpoints if needed, and **lock** each sample you are happy with.

Annotation deliberately does not happen until you have locked an assembly, so the
Annotate tab is empty until the next step.

# Step 7: Annotate the locked assemblies

Now run the annotation stage on the assemblies you locked. It marks the five
features (18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 28S) and runs the automatic quality checks.

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::run_annotate("~/my_project", conda_env = "ribopilot")
```

You can also launch this from inside the app: switch to the Annotate tab and use
the **Update** button, which shows a live progress display. If you later go back
and switch a sample to a different reconstruction, just run this step again; it
re-annotates only the samples that changed.

# Step 8: Review the annotations and curation flags

Back in the app's **Annotate tab**, open a sample to see its five features laid
out, a plot of sequencing depth, and a **Curation flags** panel. The flags are
RiboPilot's automatic quality checks, for example a missing gene, an unusual
length, a feature on the wrong strand, or a possible contaminant. Each flag links
to the feature it concerns, so you can jump straight to it and adjust the
boundaries. The [curation guide](Curation-Flags.html) explains every flag. Lock
each sample once you are happy with it.

# Step 9: Export for GenBank

Once your samples are locked in the Annotate tab, export a submission package.
You can group samples in the app's Export tab, or export everything from R:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::export_project("~/my_project")
```

The package contains the files GenBank expects, plus a convenient FASTA file for
each marker (18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 28S, and the full repeat), a summary table,
and a readable report. Any extra columns from your mapping file are carried
through onto the submission.

# The whole workflow at a glance

```{r, purl = FALSE}
RiboPilot::new_project(...)          # Step 3: set up
RiboPilot::run_assembly(project)     # Step 4: assemble (+ BLAST, coverage)
RiboPilot::run_fallback(project)     # Step 5: rescue difficult samples (optional)
RiboPilot(project)                   # Step 6: review + LOCK assemblies (Assemble tab)
RiboPilot::run_annotate(project)     # Step 7: annotate + curate locked assemblies
RiboPilot(project)                   # Step 8: review annotations + flags, lock (Annotate tab)
RiboPilot::export_project(project)   # Step 9: export
```

That is a complete project. To adapt RiboPilot to a new group of organisms, see
the [reference database guide](Reference-Databases.html). To understand the
automatic quality checks in more depth, see the
[curation guide](Curation-Flags.html).

<div class="alert alert-warning">
<strong>If assembly reports a BLAST error</strong> mentioning "GNUTLS" or "secure
session", the version of the BLAST tool in your environment is too old to connect
to NCBI. Update it by running <code>conda install -n ribopilot 'blast&gt;=2.12'</code>
in a terminal, then run the assembly step again. Environments created from the
current <code>environment.yml</code> already include a new enough version.
</div>
